fatal_errors: The proposed Cu interlayer is absent from the target system; the reported transition occurs in the λ = 16 nm Al-Cr-Fe-Ni multilayer with semicoherent FCC/BCC interfaces.
The hypothesis replaces modulation-period-controlled coherency with an unsupported compositional intervention.
It assumes elevated-temperature creep, whereas the target result was obtained by room-temperature nanoindentation creep.

It reverses the relevant baseline: the coherent M8 and grain-boundary-dominated M32/M80 samples exhibit predominantly dislocation-mediated creep, while semicoherent M16 exhibits diffusion/interface-slip signatures.
The cited evidence concerns corrosion in molten fluoride salts and provides no support for Cu-mediated coherency or creep-mechanism transitions.
The claim that high-diffusivity Cu would reduce diffusion-mediated creep is not mechanistically justified and may point in the opposite direction.
explanation: The response recognizes that interface coherency can control the balance between diffusion- and dislocation-mediated creep, but it does not reconstruct the reported material or experiment. The relevant material is the approximately 1 μm-thick FCC/BCC Al-Cr-Fe-Ni multilayer with a 16 nm modulation period (M16), whose semicoherent interfaces and misfit dislocations strongly impede glide and are proposed to promote interfacial amorphization, atomic diffusion, or interface slip. M16 showed the lowest stress exponents and strongest reported room-temperature creep resistance relative to coherent M8 and grain-boundary-dominated M32/M80. The proposed Cu study is experimentally testable as a separate hypothesis, but its rationale is unsupported by the supplied citation and does not answer the target question.
